Basic rules for noise levels
This part of the manual explains how the desk handles it
Noise levels matter at the Companion Animal Travel Desk because calm animals, calm travelers, and calm staff all do better when the space stays steady. We keep our own voices low, we avoid crowding the counter, and we remind travelers that small interruptions can unsettle a pet even when nothing else seems wrong. If a traveler arrives worried about a barking dog, a chirping carrier, or an animal that seems restless, we stay even-tempered and keep the discussion simple and practical. Aisha Petrov and Talia Okafor may each come to the desk with different concerns, but the same approach applies: listen, note the issue, and keep the tone gentle.

When an animal becomes noisy, the first step is not to rush. We check whether the carrier is secure, whether the traveler has water or comfort items ready, and whether the pet seems distressed by the surrounding noise. If the setting is busy, we move the conversation away from the line when possible. We do not raise our voices to compete with the noise, because that usually makes the whole area feel sharper. Instead, we speak clearly, give simple instructions, and let the traveler settle the pet before we continue.

For routine desk work, we keep background sounds under control as much as we can. Phones, printers, and nearby conversation should not become part of the problem. If a pet is already sensitive, we shorten the exchange and handle the paperwork in a calm order so the traveler can leave the counter without extra stress. Baxter, or any other pet in our care, should never be treated as an annoyance. The animal is part of the trip, and our job is to make the process easier, not harder.

If noise continues to build, or if a traveler cannot manage the animal safely at the counter, we move to a calm stepwise review with the cabin team and the senior coordinator. Keep the notes clear, keep the tone kind, and avoid guessing about what might happen next. If anything feels out of place, contact the senior coordinator or the duty supervisor at once.
